senses.def: pertaining to one who has not acquired a formal education (referring primarily to formal training)
senses.comment: Some persons have assumed that ἀγράμματος in Acts 4:13 means ‘illiterate’ in the sense of not being able to read or write, but this is highly unlikely in view of the almost universal literacy in NT times, and especially as the result of extensive synagogue schools. Evidently, ἀγράμματος in Acts 4:13 refers to a lack of formal rabbinic training.

senses.def: Egypt

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of ἀκρασία ‘lack of self-control,’ 88.91) pertaining to lacking self-control
the father of Ἰάκωβος[c]
the father of Λευί[a]
pertaining to being necessary and indispensable to the occurrence of some event
pertaining to a close interpersonal relation
to cause something to be unrolled
glosses: to unroll (a book in the form of) a scroll

senses.def: a person who murders another person
pertaining to preceding in a written or spoken series

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: pertaining to being qualitatively superior in view of being in a higher or better position
to keep thinking about, without having one’s attention distracted
the shape or shade cast by an object which blocks rays of light
senses.comment: In a number of languages a term for ‘shadow’ has a number of very important meanings. In some instances it is regarded as a part of personality which goes on to the next world, since a dead person no longer ‘casts a shadow.’ The shadow may also be regarded as a kind of counterpart of the personality, a type of alter ego. In cases of severe illness one may say ‘his shadow has walked away,’ and in many parts of the world the shadow of a person is an important element in the practice of black magic, for to damage a shadow may be regarded as a means of causing harm to a person.|In James 1:17 one may translate ‘shifting shadow’ as ‘a shadow which constantly changes.’

senses.def: a city in Judea
to be in a state of incapacity or weakness
senses.comment: In some languages it may be better to translate this expression in Romans 14:1 as ‘welcome those who have only a little faith.’

senses.def: to be sick and, as a result, in a state of weakness and incapacity
(derivative of αὐλός ‘flute,’ 6.87) one who plays the flute
a city in Macedonia
a relatively low elevated land formation, in contrast with ὄρος ‘mountain’ (1.46), which refers to something higher
to have descended from a particular lineage
glosses: to be in the lineage of
senses.comment: The meaning of Hebrews 7:6 may also be expressed as ‘they were not his forefathers.’

senses.def: a cryptic name to designate an enemy to be conquered by the Messiah

senses.subdomain: Instruments Used in Binding and Fastening
senses.def: any instrument or means of binding or tying; used for binding objects together or restraining prisoners
senses.comment: In translating Acts 16:26 one may often use a descriptive phrase, for example, ‘those things that bound them’ or ‘things with which they were tied.’ It is generally more satisfactory, however, to employ wherever possible a more specific referent, for example, ‘ropes,’ ‘chains’ or ‘fetters.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of δεσμός[a] ‘bonds,’ 6.14) the state of being in prison
senses.comment: The state of being a prisoner is often expressed somewhat idiomatically, for example, ‘to be tied hand and foot,’ ‘to be chained like a dog,’ or ‘to look through iron bars.’

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of δεσμός[a] ‘bond,’ 6.14) a state of physical incapacity or illness, usually as the result of some controlling supernatural force (in Luke 13:16, the result of the activity of Satan)
to make a serious declaration on the basis of presumed personal knowledge
to be emphatic in stating an opinion or desire
to admonish or instruct with regard to some future happening or action, with the implication of personal knowledge or experience
to think about something thoroughly and/or seriously
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘thinking thoroughly or seriously about something’ is merely ‘to think very much about,’ but if possible, the focus should be upon intensity rather than mere quantity.

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to deceive by using trickery and falsehood
in Hebrew
one, in contrast to more than one; cardinal number, where there is one instance of a countable entity

senses.subdomain: Whom or What Spoken or Written About
senses.def: a reference to a single, indefinite person or thing (sometimes reinforced by the indefinite reference τις[a], 92.12)
that which is united as one in contrast with being divided or consisting of separate parts
senses.comment: This phrase in Galatians 3:20 is a reference to the fact that God in the Scriptures is defined as a unit and not as being characterized by numerous manifestations or realizations.

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to make a choice of one or more possible alternatives
senses.comment: In a number of languages the choice of terms or expressions for ‘choosing’ or ‘selecting’ often depends upon either (1) what is chosen or selected or (2) the purpose for such a choice, for example, personal pleasure, rational evaluation, or outright prejudice.

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: to make a special choice based upon significant preference, often implying a strongly favorable attitude toward what is chosen
to state that someone has done wrong, with the implication that there is adequate proof of such wrongdoing
(derivative of ἐμπορεύομαι[a] ‘to engage in a business,’ 57.196) a place for engaging in business (but see ἀγορά, 57.207)
a state of oneness
senses.comment: In some languages it may be strange to speak of ‘that oneness in our faith.’ The closest equivalent may be ‘we believe just as though we were all one person’ or ‘we believe in one and the same way.’

senses.def: to be completely capable of doing or experiencing something
to reach out or stretch out toward some goal
senses.comment: In Philippians 3:13 ἐπεκτείνομαι is used figuratively to suggest intense effort as well as firm purpose.

senses.def: to attempt energetically to attain a state or condition
to swear that one will do something and then not fulfill the promise
glosses: to swear and fail to keep
senses.comment: See also 33.465.

senses.def: to take an oath that something is true, when in reality one knows that it is false
senses.comment: In the one occurrence in the NT of ἐπιορκέω[a] (33.464). In either case, it is often necessary to be quite specific about the meaning and to introduce sufficient information into the context so that the specific aspect of either breaking an oath or swearing falsely will be clear.

senses.def: to classify oneself by means of a name, title, or attribution

senses.subdomain: Acceptable To, To Be Pleased With
senses.def: to cause someone to be well-disposed toward or to be pleased with someone
a young man who fell out of a window in Troas
to cause to continue to live
senses.comment: ‘So that they could not be kept alive’ (Acts 7:19) may be rendered as ‘so that they would not continue to live’ or ‘so that they would die.’

senses.def: to cause to live
(derivative of θαῦμα[a] ‘wonder, amazement,’ 25.212) to wonder or marvel at some event or object
glosses: to marvel (whether the reaction is favorable or unfavorable depends on the context)

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to admire the face) to praise someone, normally in an exaggerated or false manner and with insincere purpose
to be in a state of fear associated with surprise
senses.comment: For the reference of διὰ πνεύματος in 2 Thessalonians 2:2, see commentaries.

senses.def: (derivative of ἱκανός[c] ‘adequate,’ 75.2) to cause someone or something to be adequate for something
John the Baptist
one of the twelve apostles and the son of Zebedee and brother of James
senses.comment: Some persons consider Ἰωάννης[b] and Ἰωάννης[c] to be the same.

senses.def: the author of the book of Revelation
senses.comment: Some persons consider Ἰωάννης[b] and Ἰωάννης[c] to be the same.

senses.def: a companion of Paul who was also called Mark
the father of Peter and Andrew
a member of the Sanhedrin
to judge someone as definitely guilty and thus subject to punishment
glosses: to render a verdict of guilt

senses.def: to make someone completely adequate or sufficient for something
glosses: to cause to be fully qualified

senses.def: to cause to suffer because of intense heat
to break an object into two or more parts (in the NT κλάω and κλάσις are used exclusively for breaking bread)
senses.comment: In some languages important distinctions are made for terms meaning ‘to break’ depending on the substance involved. For example, the breaking of a stick or a bone would require quite a different term from that used in speaking of breaking bread. Furthermore, the action of breaking bread would probably imply breaking into several pieces rather than a single break. Such a distinction may likewise require a special term.

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: hair of the head of human beings

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: pertaining to not being able to be known, in view of the fact that it has been kept secret
glosses: not able to be made known
senses.comment: In a number of languages there may be complications involved in what could be regarded as a triple negation in the sense that ‘nothing,’ ‘secret’ (in the sense of ‘not known’), and ‘not be made known’ are all semantic negations. It may therefore be better to render Matthew 10:26 as ‘everything that is now not known will be made known.’|In a number of languages ‘secret’ is regularly expressed as ‘not known’ or ‘what is kept from being known.’

senses.def: (idiom, literally: the hidden (person)) the psychological faculty, including intellectual, emotional, and spiritual aspects, in contrast with the purely physical aspects of human existence
senses.comment: A strictly literal rendering of ἀλλ ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ Ἰουδαῖος might be misunderstood in Romans 2:29 to refer only to the fact of circumcision, which would be something which would normally not be evident.|In a number of languages it is quite impossible to speak of the psychological faculty of a person as being merely ‘that which is within.’ It is frequently necessary to refer to a particular organ of the body, for example, ‘the heart’ or ‘the liver’ or ‘the spleen.’ In some languages, however, one may refer to this faculty as being ‘the person who stands inside’ or ‘the real person’ or even ‘the other person.’|In Luke 17:21 the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in the statement ἰδοὺ γὰρ ἡ βασιλεία τοῦ θεοῦ ἐντὸς ὑμῶν ἐστιν ‘look, God’s reign is within you’ may constitute a reference to the same inner being designated by the phrases ὁ ἔσω and ὁ ἐν τῷ κρυπτῷ. On this basis some scholars have suggested that the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν can be interpreted as a potentiality for participation and hence be translated ‘within your grasp,’ but it is more likely that one should understand the phrase ἐντὸς ὑμῶν in Luke 17:21 as a spacial relationship, for example, ‘in your midst’ or ‘among you’ (see 83.9).

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: the content of what is not able to be known

senses.subdomain: Not Able To Be Known, Secret
senses.def: pertaining to not being able to be known by the public but known by some in-group or by those immediately involved

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to living in ostentatious luxury
senses.comment: The equivalent of λαμπρῶς in the sense of ‘luxuriously’ may be rendered in a number of languages as ‘richly’ or ‘with things which cost a great deal’ or ‘with more possessions than one can count.’

senses.def: pertaining to being genuine, in the sense of being true to the real and essential nature of something
senses.comment: Since in 1 Peter 2:2 the context is figurative, some translators have preferred to render λογικός as ‘spiritual,’ so as to make the reference not literal but figurative.

senses.def: a Roman province in Greece
to cause something to be moved from one place to another
senses.comment: It is not possible to determine whether in 1 Corinthians 13:2 one should understand ‘remove mountains’ in the sense of ‘causing them to disappear’ or ‘to cause a mountain to change its location,’ that is to say, to move a mountain from one place to another.

senses.def: to cause a change of state, with emphasis upon the difference in the resulting state
glosses: to cause to be different from

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of μεθίστημι[a] ‘to cause to move,’ 15.9) to cause a complete change in someone’s beliefs, normally in the unfavorable sense of causing someone to turn away from a previous belief and hence to be misled
to cease from a state or function, with the implication of transfer or removal
senses.comment: See also μεθίστημι[b] in 13.64.

senses.def: to effect a change of location in space, with the implication that the two locations are significantly different
glosses: to move from one place to another

senses.def: to cause a change of state, with emphasis upon the difference in the resulting state
glosses: to cause to be different from

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to change from) to abandon an association
to recall information from memory, but without necessarily the implication that persons have actually forgotten
senses.comment: In some languages the process of remembering is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to find one’s thoughts again’ or ‘to see again in one’s heart’ or ‘to have one’s liver repeat the words.’

senses.def: a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a formalized rule (or set of rules) prescribing what people must do
senses.comment: The difference between ‘a law’ and ‘a command’ is that a law is enforced by sanctions from a society, while a command carries only the sanctions of the individual who commands. When, however, the people of Israel accepted the commands of God as the rules which they would follow and enforce, these became their laws.|The occurrence of νόμος two times in Romans 8:2 poses certain problems of both translation and interpretation: ὁ γὰρ νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ ἠλευθέρωσέν σε ἀπὸ τοῦ νόμου τῆς ἁμαρτίας καὶ τοῦ θανάτου ‘for the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus freed you from the law which leads to sin and death.’ In the second occurrence of νόμος, the meaning is clearly the rules and regulations of the OT law, but in the case of the first occurrence of νόμος, there is no such formulation of decrees. The reference in this instance must therefore be to certain basic principles. If, however, one understands νόμος in the sense of a type of abstract ‘governing power,’ it is possible that the reference in the phrase νόμος τοῦ πνεύματος τῆς ζωῆς is to this governing power of the Spirit of life which frees one from the law which stipulates sin and death.

senses.def: the first five books of the OT called the Torah (often better rendered as ‘instruction’)
senses.comment: In a number of languages it is not possible to use a singular expression such as ‘the Law,’ for since the Torah consisted of five books and included a number of regulations and instructions, it is necessary in many languages to use ‘the laws.’ Furthermore, to distinguish this body of laws from common, ordinary customs or legal regulations, it may be necessary to employ a phrase such as ‘the laws given to Moses’ or simply ‘the laws of Moses.’

senses.def: the sacred writings of the OT
senses.comment: It is clear from the content of the quotation in John 10:34 that the reference of νόμος is not restricted to the first five books of the OT, for the passage comes from the Psalms.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: law of the man, or: law of the husband) the law which binds a woman to a man in marriage
senses.comment: It may be especially difficult in some languages to speak of ‘being free from the marriage law.’ An appropriate equivalent in some languages may be ‘she is no longer obliged to remain the wife of the dead man,’ but in other languages it is more meaningful to say ‘she is then permitted to marry another man.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the Law and the Prophets) all of the sacred writings of the OT, including the Law, the Prophets, and the Writings
a building or place where one dwells
senses.comment: The size of an οἰκία[a] or of an οἶκος[a] (7.2) may differ greatly. For example, the house referred to in Luke 7:10 would no doubt have been relatively elaborate, and in Matthew 11:8 οἶκος[a] refers to the palace in which Herod lived. In a number of languages it is important to distinguish clearly between various types of dwellings depending upon their size and presumed importance. Accordingly, in rendering οἰκία[a] or οἶκος[a] it is necessary to use a number of different terms roughly equivalent to the English series ‘cottage,’ ‘house,’ ‘official residence,’ ‘palace,’ ‘temple,’ etc.|In a number of languages one must distinguish carefully between a house and a home. A term meaning ‘house’ would be used in referring to any dwelling as a construction, while a term meaning ‘home’ would be used in referring to the more or less permanent dwelling of a particular person. In Mark 2:1, for example, it is significant to indicate that Jesus was dwelling in the house through the roof of which the paralyzed man was let down.

senses.subdomain: Groups and Members of Groups of Persons Regarded as Related by Blood but without Special Reference to Successive Generations
senses.def: the family consisting of those related by blood and marriage, as well as slaves and servants, living in the same house or homestead
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of οἶκος[b] or οἰκία[b] would be ‘those who live together’ or ‘those who have the same fence’ (this being a reference to a group of huts surrounded by a fence and thus constituting a single so-called ‘family unit’).

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of οἰκία[a] ‘house,’ 7.3) possessions associated with a house and household
senses.comment: It is also possible in Mark 12:40 to understand τὰς οἰκίας as meaning specifically ‘houses.’

senses.def: pertaining to being of the same mind or having the same thoughts as someone else
senses.comment: In some languages it may be better to speak of ‘having the same attitudes’ or, idiomatically, ‘having thoughts that follow the same path.’

senses.def: a relative reference to any entity, event, or state, either occurring overtly in the immediate context or clearly implied in the discourse or setting
a marker of an explanation or a clarification in the same or a different language
senses.comment: In some languages one must make more specific the interpretation of a term in another language. For example, in Mark 3:17 it may be necessary to translate ‘Boanerges, which in another language means Men of Thunder’ or ‘Boanerges, for which we would say, Men of Thunder.’

senses.def: to experience strong physical desires, particularly of a sexual nature
to cause someone to be encouraged or consoled, either by verbal or non-verbal means
to ask for something earnestly and with propriety
to cause to be in a place
to cause something to be or to serve as
to cause to come into existence
to make something available to someone without necessarily involving actual change of ownership

to deliver a person into the control of someone else, involving either the handing over of a presumably guilty person for punishment by authorities or the handing over of an individual to an enemy who will presumably take undue advantage of the victim
senses.comment: As is the case in English, a number of languages make a clear distinction between legitimate handing over of a presumably guilty person to a civil authority and the betrayal of a person in the in-group to someone in the out-group.

senses.def: to establish evidence to show that something is true

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to stand near or alongside of someone, either with friendly or hostile intent
senses.comment: To indicate merely that the kings of the earth were present may not be sufficient to communicate satisfactorily the hostile intent implied by the context of Acts 4:26. It may therefore be important to translate ‘the kings of earth prepared themselves’ or even ‘the kings of earth armed themselves.’

senses.def: to be in proximity to something
to be in front of something, presumably facing it
senses.comment: The actual body stance in translating παρίστημι[i] is not crucial to the meaning; the focus in Acts 27:24 is simply upon the position in front of the emperor.

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: to occur at a particular or expected time
to come to be present at a particular place
to assist in supplying what may be needed

senses.subdomain: Once, Twice, Three Times, Etc. [Cardinals of Time]
senses.def: five occurrences
to cause a change of state, with emphasis upon the difference in the resulting state
glosses: to cause to be different from

senses.def: the movement of a boat or ship through the water, either rowed or blown by the wind
one who frequently travels by sea
the experience of pain, normally involving both continuity and intensity
senses.comment: In a number of languages it may not be possible, or at least it may not be natural, to use nouns for ‘death,’ ‘grief,’ ‘crying,’ or ‘pain.’ Corresponding verb expressions may, however, be employed, for example, ‘people will no longer die, will no longer grieve, will no longer cry, and will no longer be in pain’ or ‘… suffer pain.’

senses.def: hard work, implying accompanying pain and distress

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to sin previously or in the past
to spend excessively

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of προσωπολημπτέω ‘to show favoritism,’ 88.238) one who unjustly treats one person better than another
fiery red
senses.comment: One may also render ‘fiery red’ as ‘red like fire’ or ‘the color of fire.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: lines or creases in the skin
senses.comment: In Ephesians 5:27 ῥυτίς is used symbolically as a type of imperfection, but in some languages wrinkles can be an evidence of age and therefore of seniority and even wisdom

senses.def: a sudden and severe movement of the earth
senses.comment: Since earthquakes are universal in occurrence, there is normally no difficulty involved in finding some way of speaking about them. However, in a number of languages idiomatic expressions are used, for example, ‘the devil rolled over’ or ‘mother earth belched.’|In Acts 16:26 the earthquake is regarded as the cause of the prison foundations shaking, and it may be better to restructure the relationships expressed in Acts 16:26 as ‘the prison shook because of the earthquake.’

senses.subdomain: Events Involving Liquids and Dry Masses
senses.def: a violent action of the surface of a body of water as the result of high waves caused by a strong wind
senses.comment: Though the term σεισμός[b] obviously implies the strong action of the wind, the focus is upon the violent motion caused by the waves. It might, therefore, be more appropriate to translate Matthew 8:24 as ‘there were huge waves on the sea’ or ‘… on the lake.’ Such a translation would then be appropriate for the following clause.

senses.def: a dwelling, with the implication of temporary duration
senses.comment: In Acts 7:46 there is a complex textual problem in which the critical text has τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰακώβ ‘the house of Jacob’ (but in the figurative sense of ‘people’), but the Byzantine text reads τῷ θεῷ Ἰακώβ ‘the God of Jacob.’ It is only with this latter form of the text that σκήνωμα would mean an actual construction or dwelling. If one adopts the form of the critical text, then σκήνωμα would point to ‘a place to dwell,’ in other words, an area or region (see 85.77).

senses.def: (derivative of σκηνόω ‘to take up residence,’ 85.75) a place where one may dwell, with the possible implication in certain contexts of something which is of temporary duration
senses.comment: An alternative reading of the expression σκήνωμα τῷ οἴκῳ Ἰακώβ ‘dwelling place for the people of Jacob’ in Acts 7:46 has θεῷ for οἴκῳ (see 7.8) and the consequent translation ‘a house for the God of Jacob.’|For another interpretation of σκήνωμα in 2 Peter 1:14, see 8.5.

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of σκήνωμα[a] ‘temporary dwelling,’ 7.8) temporary habitation in the human body
senses.comment: Only rarely can one preserve in translation the figurative meanings suggested by the terms σκῆνος and σκήνωμα. What is significant in such contexts is the temporary nature of the dwelling, and therefore the relatively brief time which the body is to serve the person who dwells in it. In some cases it may be relevant, therefore, to have a footnote to point out the temporal aspects of this figurative usage of σκῆνος and σκήνωμα[c].|It is also possible to interpret σκήνωμα in 2 Peter 1:14 as meaning a temporary habitation, though referring, of course, to the human body (see 85.77).

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be in a dwelling, see 7.8) to be alive, with special emphasis upon physical existence on earth
senses.comment: Most languages have rather generic expressions for ‘life’ or ‘to live,’ but sometimes there are idiomatic expressions which may readily fit the types of contexts illustrated by 2 Corinthians 5:6 and 2 Peter 1:13, for example, ‘to have strength,’ ‘to have one’s eyes,’ and ‘to walk about on the earth.’

senses.def: to do something hurriedly, with the implication of associated energy
to do something with intense effort and motivation

senses.subdomain: Be Eager, Be Earnest, In a Devoted Manner
senses.def: to be eager to do something, with the implication of readiness to expend energy and effort
to spread something out
to fit out or arrange a room in a suitable manner (that is, to provide it with necessary furniture)
to prepare a bed, either for sleeping or making it up after it has been used
(derivative of συμμετέχω ‘to share in the possession of something,’ not occurring in the NT) one who shares in a possession or a relationship
to be aware of information about something
(contrast συνείδησις[a] ‘knowledge about something,’ 28.4) the psychological faculty which can distinguish between right and wrong
senses.comment: In some languages συνείδησις[b] may be rendered as ‘the inner voice’ or ‘the voice in one’s heart’ or ‘how one knows right from wrong.’ In some instances συνείδησις[b] may be equivalent to some organ of the body, for example, heart or liver, but generally some descriptive phrase proves to be the most satisfactory equivalent.

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to be seared in the conscience, or: to be seared as to one’s conscience) to be unwilling to learn from one’s conscience
glosses: to refuse to listen to one’s conscience

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: to extend in time, with focus upon the end point
to remove from a place by taking away or carrying away
senses.comment: In Acts 5:6 συστέλλω may also be interpreted as meaning ‘to wrap up’ (see 79.119).

senses.def: to wrap up an object, with the implication of getting it ready to remove
senses.comment: For another interpretation of συστέλλω in Acts 5:6, see 15.200.

senses.subdomain: Regions Below the Surface of the Earth
senses.def: (derivative of τάρταρος ‘Tartarus,’ ‘hell,’ as a place of torture or torment, not occurring in the NT) to cast into or to cause to remain in Tartarus
senses.comment: In many cases it is confusing to add still another term for a designation of hell by transliterating the Greek τάρταρος, and so most translators have preferred to render ταρταρόω as either ‘to cast into hell’ or ‘to keep in hell,’ thus using for ‘hell’ the same term as is employed for a rendering of the Greek term γέεννα (1.21).

senses.subdomain: Honor or Respect in Relation to Status
senses.def: to attribute high status to someone by honoring
to determine an amount to be used in paying for something
senses.comment: It would also be possible to translate ‘the price set on him by the people of Israel’ as ‘the amount the people of Israel had agreed to pay for him.’

senses.def: to provide aid or financial assistance, with the implication that this is an appropriate means of showing respect
glosses: to provide for the needs of as a sign of respect

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of τροχός ‘wheel,’ not occurring in the NT) an ordered series of events, involving repeated patterns
senses.comment: For another interpretation of τροχός in James 3:6, see 67.83.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of τροχός ‘wheel,’ not occurring in the NT) a period of time of indefinite length, characterized by recurring events or patterns
senses.comment: In some languages τὸν τροχὸν τῆς γενέσεως may be best rendered as ‘the very way in which we live’ or ‘the manner of our life.’ For another interpretation of τροχός in James 3:6, see 61.5.

senses.def: submission to the orders or directives of someone
a state of ruin or destruction, with the implication of disintegration
senses.comment: In 2 Peter 2:12 it may be more appropriate in a number of languages to translate ‘… to be killed.’

senses.def: to rot or decay, in reference to organic matter

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: a state of moral corruption and depravity
senses.comment: In some languages ‘slaves of moral corruption’ in 2 Peter 2:19 may be expressed as ‘their immoral desires make slaves of them’ or ‘… cause them to be slaves.’

senses.subdomain: Hold a Wrong View, Be Mistaken
senses.def: (derivative of φρεναπατάω ‘to lead astray,’ 31.12) one who misleads people concerning the truth
senses.comment: In some languages the equivalent of φρεναπάτης is ‘one who leads along the wrong path’ or ‘one who says wrong is right.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to show kindness to someone, with the implication of graciousness on the part of the one showing such kindness
senses.comment: It is important to note that kindness in English indicates an activity in which an individual is kind to someone; it is essentially an event involving a particular quality. The same is true of χάρις in Acts 15:40, for this is not a mere gracious disposition, but an expectation of the Lord’s showing kindness.

senses.subdomain: Precious and Semiprecious Stones and Substances
